newsitem.title: BRAZIL: U.N. rights representative criticizes Burundi.
newsitem.headline: U.N. rights representative criticizes Burundi.

text.p: A U.N. human rights investigator accused by Burundi of producing politically slanted reports criticised the African nation again on Friday, saying six people executed on Thursday might not have received a fair trial.

Paulo Sergio Pinheiro, a Brazilian university professor, also told Reuters his earlier criticisms of conditions in camps in Burundi were accurate, despite claims to the contrary by Burundi's government.
"The (Burundi) government has every right to criticise my reports but to complain of a political slant just does not correspond with reality," Pinheiro said.
"What possible political party position could I have regarding Burundi? My only position is on the side of the victims."
Earlier Friday, a U.N. spokeswoman said Pinheiro would not be replaced as its human rights envoy to Burundi, rejecting demands from Bujumbura that he be sacked.

Pinheiro, speaking by telephone from Sao Paulo, said Thursday's execution of six people accused of playing a leading role in 1993 inter-ethnic genocide was a "grave step" and would feature in a new report he was drawing up for the U.N.

"The fact that six people were executed is a grave step, and I believe they were not given access to proper defence lawyers. In several cases the trials lasted two hours without defence lawyers," he said.

The six, three Hutus, two Tutsis and one ethnic Twa, included a former school headmaster accused of burning more than a dozen pupils alive in his schoolroom, according to a statement by Burundi's justice ministry.
Pinheiro said dozens of other people accused of taking part in the wave of ethnic killings that swept Burundi four years ago had been sentenced to death and were due to be executed.

Pinheiro, a social science professor at the University of Sao Paulo, was appointed as the U.N.'s human rights investigator in Burundi in 1995. Since then he has visited the tiny African country three times.

Diplomats at the U.N. said Thursday that Burundi's foreign minister Luc Rukingama had complained of a political slant in Pinheiro's reports, which were critical of the military government's policy of forcing rural populations into camps.
Rukingama was also said to have criticised Pinheiro for not visiting Burundi since Tutsi military leader Pierre Buyoya took power in a coup a year ago.
Pinheiro responded by saying he had planned to visit Burundi in July, the only month when he was free of his teaching obligations, but the African state refused him a visa.
"It was the Burundi government that would not let me in the country so their allegations are ungrounded," he said.

Pinheiro said his reports were based on information from U.N. workers in Burundi. His criticisms of Burundi's camps and the conditions inside them were also matched by a recent Amnesty International report, he said.
